category: PSpice simulation profile settings, simulation part properties, batch/modeling utilities and Advanced Analysis
description: The Simulation Settings dialog tabs and the newer .OPTIONS entries they expose (SPEED_LEVEL, THREADS, convergence flags, integration method, TRTOL, CSHUNT, LIMIT), the Capture part properties that make a symbol simulatable (PSPICETEMPLATE, IO_LEVEL, MNTYMXDLY, PSPICEDEFAULTNET, PARAM, SUBPARAM), bias point display, batch and utility programs (psp_cmd, PSpiceEnc, Magnetic Parts Editor, DMI Template Code Generator), and PSpice Advanced Analysis tools, properties and files (Sensitivity, Monte Carlo, optimizer engines, Parametric Plotter, Assign Tolerance, design variables table, Smoke derating, .aap/.drt/.table/.prp).

tools.name: Simulation Settings > General tab
tools.description: Names the profile, selects the simulation input (a Capture design and its top-level schematic, or a stand-alone .cir circuit file), and sets the output .out file and waveform .dat file names plus a free-text description. For circuit-file input the Analysis tab is disabled and analyses come from the .cir text.
tools.usage: PSpice > Edit Simulation Profile (Capture) or Simulation > Edit Profile (PSpice) > General

parameters.name: Input: Schematic / Circuit File
parameters.description: Design-based or .cir-based simulation.

parameters.name: Output Filename / Waveform Data Filename
parameters.description: Names of the .out and .dat files.

tools.example: General tab > Circuit File > C:\sims\filter.cir to simulate a hand-written netlist with the same profile machinery.

tools.name: Simulation Settings > Configuration Files tab (Library, Stimulus, Include)
tools.description: Configures model libraries, stimulus files and include files at three scopes: global (all designs), design, or profile. PSpice searches profile-level files first, then design, then global, in list order within each level, so the same circuit can be simulated with different model libraries or stimuli per profile.
tools.usage: Simulation Settings > Configuration Files > Category: Library | Stimulus | Include > Browse > Add as Global | Add to Design | Add to Profile; Change, Remove, Move up/down; Include: Edit

parameters.name: Add to Profile
parameters.description: File used only by this profile (projects created with Capture 10.0 or later).

parameters.name: Search order
parameters.description: Changeable only within the same level.

tools.example: Profile AC: Add to Profile FRQCHK.LIB; profile TRAN: Add to Profile FRQCHK_1.LIB, so each analysis uses a different DECODER model.
tools.notes: A file added at design level cannot also be added at profile level. Typical errors 'Model ... is undefined' or 'Can't find .STIMULUS definition' mean the file is missing from this list or not on the library path.

tools.name: Library Path (profile model library search path)
tools.description: Semicolon-separated list of directories PSpice searches for globally configured model libraries, shown in the Library category of the Configuration Files tab and stored as LIBPATH in pspice.ini. Adding a company model directory here avoids absolute paths in every profile.
tools.usage: Configuration Files > Library > Library Path: "<dir1>";"<dir2>"
tools.example: "C:\Cadence\SPB_17.4\tools\pspice\library";"D:\company\pspice_models"
tools.notes: Do not end the list with a semicolon. The default installation path contains the standard libraries and nom.lib.

tools.name: Simulation Settings > Options tab (Analog Simulation, Analog Advanced, Gate-level Simulation, Output file)
tools.description: Front end for the .OPTIONS statement, grouped into four categories: Analog Simulation (speed level, tolerances, GMIN, iteration limits, TNOM, threads, MOSFET defaults), Analog Advanced (convergence flags, pivot and solver settings, integration method, TRTOL, CSHUNT), Gate-level Simulation (digital timing, I/O level, drive strengths, error limits) and Output file (ACCT, EXPAND, LIST, NOBIAS, NOECHO, NUMDGT, WIDTH and similar).
tools.usage: Simulation Settings > Options > Category list; AutoConverge button suggests relaxed limits

parameters.name: AutoConverge
parameters.description: Lets PSpice relax selected limits during a run to achieve convergence; Restart restarts the convergence calculation.

tools.example: Options > Analog Simulation > RELTOL 0.001 -> 0.003 and enable AutoConverge for a hard-switching converter that stops with 'timestep too small'.
tools.notes: Every setting maps to an .OPTIONS name listed in the PSpice Reference Guide; see the individual option entries.

tools.name: SPEED_LEVEL (option)
tools.description: Analog Simulation option that increases simulation performance by optimising the switching behaviour of models; the default is 3. Set SPEED_LEVEL=0 when the extra speed is not needed and maximum fidelity to the original algorithms is preferred.
tools.usage: .OPTIONS SPEED_LEVEL=<0..3>  (Options tab > Analog Simulation > General)

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: 0 disables the speed optimisation; default 3.

tools.example: .OPTIONS SPEED_LEVEL=0
tools.notes: If a result changes noticeably between SPEED_LEVEL=3 and 0, tighten RELTOL/step size before trusting either.

tools.name: THREADS (option)
tools.description: Number of CPU threads the analog solver uses. THREADS=0 (default and recommended) lets PSpice use as many threads as detected cores; any other value is used exactly.
tools.usage: .OPTIONS THREADS=<n>

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: 0 = automatic, otherwise the thread count.

tools.example: .OPTIONS THREADS=4   (leave cores free while running several batch jobs)

tools.name: ADVCONV and PREORDER (convergence flags)
tools.description: Analog Simulation flag options: ADVCONV enables all advanced convergence algorithms such as pseudo-transient, GMIN stepping and source stepping and is ON by default; PREORDER presorts the matrix diagonal by Markowitz counts, which can help ill-conditioned circuits.
tools.usage: .OPTIONS ADVCONV  |  .OPTIONS PREORDER
tools.example: .OPTIONS ADVCONV PREORDER
tools.notes: The PSpice 17.4 help spells the second flag 'PREODER' in one table; the option name is PREORDER.

tools.name: NOGMINI / BRKDEPSRC / CONVAID / NOSTEPSRC / NOSTEPDEP / GMINSRC / PSEUDOTRAN / TRANCONV (Analog Advanced flags)
tools.description: Analog Advanced flag options controlling convergence aids: NOGMINI stops adding GMIN across current sources; BRKDEPSRC sets automatic breakpoints for behavioural sources; CONVAID writes a .1OP debug file when convergence fails; NOSTEPSRC and NOSTEPDEP disable source stepping and dependent-source stepping for the bias point; GMINSRC enables GMIN stepping inside source stepping; PSEUDOTRAN uses the pseudo-transient method; TRANCONV enables an alternate path search when transient simulation fails.
tools.usage: .OPTIONS <flag> [<flag> ...]  (Options tab > Analog Advanced)

parameters.name: CONVAID
parameters.description: Produces a .1OP file to debug bias-point failures.

parameters.name: PSEUDOTRAN
parameters.description: Finds the operating point by a pseudo-transient ramp.

tools.example: .OPTIONS CONVAID PSEUDOTRAN BRKDEPSRC
tools.notes: Change one flag at a time and compare results; several flags trade robustness for speed.

tools.name: GMINSTEPS / ITL6 / PTRANSTEP (bias point stepping options)
tools.description: Numeric Analog Advanced options for the bias-point convergence algorithms: GMINSTEPS is the number of GMIN stepping steps, ITL6 the number of source-stepping steps, and PTRANSTEP the number of pseudo-transient steps used to find the operating point. Each defaults to the ITL1 value, and 0 selects the engine default.
tools.usage: .OPTIONS GMINSTEPS=<n> ITL6=<n> PTRANSTEP=<n>
tools.example: .OPTIONS GMINSTEPS=200 ITL6=200

tools.name: METHOD (integration method option)
tools.description: Selects the transient numerical integration method, TRAPEZOIDAL or GEAR. Gear integration damps the numerical ringing that the trapezoidal rule can produce on stiff or switching circuits, at some cost in accuracy for lightly damped resonances.
tools.usage: .OPTIONS METHOD=TRAPEZOIDAL | GEAR
tools.example: .OPTIONS METHOD=GEAR
tools.notes: If an inductor current or capacitor voltage shows point-to-point zig-zag ringing, try GEAR before changing tolerances.

tools.name: TRTOL (option)
tools.description: Transient truncation-error tolerance factor, default 7. Higher values allow larger time steps and less accuracy; it should not exceed 1/RELTOL.
tools.usage: .OPTIONS TRTOL=<value>
tools.example: .OPTIONS TRTOL=1   (tighter local truncation error control for an oscillator)

tools.name: CSHUNT (option)
tools.description: Adds a shunt capacitance from every node of the design to ground; default 0, recommended value about 1 pF when used. It removes floating high-impedance nodes and sharp discontinuities that stall transient convergence.
tools.usage: .OPTIONS CSHUNT=<farads>
tools.example: .OPTIONS CSHUNT=1p
tools.notes: It changes the circuit slightly; check that high-speed or high-impedance nodes are not affected.

tools.name: LIMIT (option)
tools.description: Absolute voltage limit for data values. The default 0 means no limit; setting a large value such as 1e12 prevents overflow errors, especially with exponential sources or behavioural expressions.
tools.usage: .OPTIONS LIMIT=<value>
tools.example: .OPTIONS LIMIT=1e12

tools.name: WCDEVIATION / DIODECJO / DIODERS / BJTCJ (advanced numeric options)
tools.description: Analog Advanced numeric options: WCDEVIATION sets the worst-case deviation (0 to 1, default same as RELTOL); DIODECJO and DIODERS impose minimum diode junction capacitance and ohmic resistance; BJTCJ sets a minimum for the BJT CJC, CJE and CJS zero-bias depletion capacitances. The minimum values keep idealised models numerically well behaved.
tools.usage: .OPTIONS WCDEVIATION=<0..1> DIODECJO=<F> DIODERS=<ohm> BJTCJ=<F>
tools.example: .OPTIONS DIODECJO=1p DIODERS=1m

tools.name: Simulation Settings > Data Collection tab
tools.description: Limits which voltages, currents, power, digital and noise data are written to the .dat file (All, All but Internal Subcircuits, At Markers Only, None), chooses the ASCII CSDF format instead of binary, and sets Probe data accuracy to 64-bit (default) or 32-bit.
tools.usage: Simulation Settings > Data Collection

parameters.name: At Markers Only
parameters.description: Stores only marked quantities: smallest files for large designs.

parameters.name: Save data in the CSDF format (.CSD)
parameters.description: Portable ASCII waveform file.

parameters.name: Probe Data 32/64-bit
parameters.description: 64-bit avoids resolution 'ramps' when a small signal rides on a large one.

tools.example: Large Monte Carlo on a board-level design: Voltages = At Markers Only, Currents = None, Power = None.
tools.notes: Anything not collected cannot be plotted or measured later without re-simulating.

tools.name: Simulation Settings > Probe Window tab
tools.description: Per-profile control of the waveform window: display the Probe window when the profile is opened, during simulation (live updating) or after completion, and show traces for all markers on open schematics or the last plot used.
tools.usage: Simulation Settings > Probe Window

parameters.name: Display Probe window during simulation / after simulation has completed
parameters.description: Live or post-run display.

parameters.name: Show: All markers on open schematics / Last plot
parameters.description: Which traces appear initially.

tools.example: Choose 'after simulation has completed' and 'Last plot' for repetitive regression runs.

tools.name: .sim (PSpice simulation profile file)
tools.description: Simulation profile saved per schematic in <project>\<design>-PSpiceFiles\<root schematic>\<profile>\<profile>.sim, holding the analysis setup, options, configured files and Probe settings. PSpice opens it with File > Open Simulation and it can be imported to create profiles in other projects.
tools.usage: PSpice: File > Open Simulation > <profile>.sim; File > New > Simulation Profile > Inherit from an existing profile (.sim)
tools.example: D:\proj\amp-PSpiceFiles\SCHEMATIC1\TRAN\TRAN.sim
tools.notes: Deleting a profile in the Capture Project Manager does not delete this folder; remove it manually to reuse the name.

tools.name: .csd (CSDF waveform data file)
tools.description: Common Simulation Data Format: an ASCII alternative to the binary .dat waveform file, written when 'Save data in the CSDF format' is set. It survives transfer between platforms and is easy to parse, at the cost of size and load speed.
tools.usage: Simulation Settings > Data Collection > Save data in the CSDF format (.CSD)
tools.example: Enable CSDF, run, then parse design.csd with a Python script for automated checks.

tools.name: PSPICETEMPLATE (part property)
tools.description: Part property defining the netlist line Capture writes for the part. Regular text is copied verbatim; @prop inserts a required property value, &prop an optional one, ?prop|text| and ~prop|text| emit text if a property is defined or undefined, #prop|..| deletes the rest if undefined, %pin inserts the connected net, ^ the hierarchical path and \n a new line. Every simulatable part needs it, starting with the correct device letter.
tools.usage: PSPICETEMPLATE = <letter>^@REFDES %<pin1> %<pin2> ... [@VALUE | model | PARAMS: ...]

parameters.name: @<id> / &<id>
parameters.description: Value of property (error if missing) / value if defined.

parameters.name: ?<id>s..s / ~<id>s..s
parameters.description: Conditional text using separators , . ; / |

parameters.name: %<pin>
parameters.description: Net on the named pin; %% gives a literal %.

tools.example:
R^@REFDES %1 %2 @VALUE
V^@REFDES %+ %- ?DC|DC=@DC| ?AC|AC=@AC|
X^@REFDES %a %b Z PARAMS: ?G|G=@G||G=1000|
tools.notes: Pin names in the template must match the part pins and the node order of the .SUBCKT. Capture translates < > = in pin names to l g e.

tools.name: IO_LEVEL / MNTYMXDLY / PSPICEDEFAULTNET (digital part properties)
tools.description: Simulation properties for digital parts: IO_LEVEL selects the AtoD/DtoA interface subcircuit level (0 circuit default, 1-4 AtoDn/DtoAn), MNTYMXDLY selects the propagation delay set (0 default, 1 min, 2 typ, 3 max, 4 worst-case min/max), and PSPICEDEFAULTNET on an invisible power or ground pin names the net it connects to, e.g. $G_DPWR.
tools.usage: Part properties used inside PSPICETEMPLATE: IO_LEVEL=<0..4>  MNTYMXDLY=<0..4>  pin property PSPICEDEFAULTNET=<net>
tools.example: Set MNTYMXDLY=4 on a critical 74HC74 to run it with worst-case min/max timing while the rest uses typical delays.

tools.name: PARAM part (global parameters in Capture)
tools.description: Part from SPECIAL.OLB that declares global parameters on the schematic. Each new property on the PARAM instance becomes a parameter name with its default value, and any value on the schematic can then reference it in braces, which is what DC, parametric and Monte Carlo sweeps of design variables operate on.
tools.usage: Place > Part > SPECIAL.OLB > PARAM; Edit > Properties > New Property <name> = <value>; use {<name>} in part values
tools.example: PARAM with RLOAD=1k; load resistor VALUE={RLOAD}; Parametric Sweep > Global parameter RLOAD 100 10k dec 5
tools.notes: Display the property as Name and Value so the defaults are visible. Do not use reserved system-variable names (TEMP, VT, GMIN...).

tools.name: SUBPARAM part (parameters for hierarchical subcircuits)
tools.description: Part from SPECIAL.OLB placed on a child schematic that is netlisted as a subcircuit. Its properties define parameter names and defaults that parts inside the child can use in their templates, and that parent instances can override, giving parameterised hierarchical blocks.
tools.usage: In the subcircuit schematic: Place > Part > SUBPARAM (SPECIAL.OLB); Edit > Properties to add <param>=<default>
tools.example: Child filter schematic: SUBPARAM with FC=1k; capacitor VALUE={1/(6.2832*FC*10k)}; parent block instance FC=5k.

tools.name: Bias point display (Enable Bias Voltage / Current / Power Display)
tools.description: After a simulation that computes a bias point, Capture can annotate the schematic with node voltages, device currents and power dissipation directly on the page. Individual values can be shown or hidden, which makes quick DC debugging possible without opening the output file.
tools.usage: Capture PSpice toolbar V / I / W buttons (Enable Bias Voltage Display, Enable Bias Current Display, Enable Bias Power Display), or the PSpice > Bias Points submenu
tools.example: Run a Bias Point profile, click V and I on the toolbar, and check that the transistor collector sits near mid-supply.
tools.notes: Values shown are from the last bias point (for transient profiles, the initial operating point). The full table is in the .out file.

tools.name: psp_cmd.exe (non-interactive batch simulation)
tools.description: Command-line PSpice executable that runs a circuit file in the background without opening the PSpice GUI; it sits next to pspice.exe. On non-convergence it waits 10 s for user intervention and then proceeds, which suits unattended batch scripts; pspice.exe /r is the interactive alternative.
tools.usage: <CDS_INST_DIR>\tools\pspice\psp_cmd.exe /r <circuit.cir>

parameters.name: /r
parameters.description: Run the simulation.

tools.example: for %f in (C:\sims\*.cir) do "%CDSROOT%\tools\pspice\psp_cmd.exe" /r "%f"
tools.notes: Generate the .cir/.net first (run once from Capture or PSpice > Create Netlist); results land in the .out and .dat next to the .cir.

tools.name: PSpiceEnc (model encryption utility)
tools.description: Command-line utility that encrypts PSpice model libraries so vendors can distribute models that simulate without revealing their contents; the same capability is exposed in the Model Editor. From 16.6 the default mode is AES-256, while older DES-encrypted models remain readable; user-defined keys come from a CSV file referenced by an environment variable.
tools.usage: PSpiceEnc [-e | -i | -n | -p] [-mode n] <inputFilePath> <outputFilePath>

parameters.name: -mode 0
parameters.description: Pre-16.6 (16.5) scheme.

parameters.name: -mode 2
parameters.description: DES with advanced data security.

parameters.name: -mode 3
parameters.description: AES (default from 16.6).

parameters.name: -e / -i / -n / -p
parameters.description: Encryption-content switches documented with the release; see PSpiceEnc help for which parts (e.g. interface) stay visible.

tools.example: PSpiceEnc -mode 3 mymodels.lib mymodels_enc.lib
tools.notes: User keys: environment variable CDS_PSPICE_ENCKEYS pointing to a CSV of key pairs (spelled CDN_PSPICE_ENCKEYS in some later sources; check your release). Encrypted text cannot be edited in Model Editor.

tools.name: Magnetic Parts Editor
tools.description: PSpice accessory for designing transformers and inductors for switched-mode power supplies (forward and flyback converters). It selects cores, bobbins, wire and insulation from a database of commercial parts (extensible by the user), computes the winding design, generates a manufacturer data sheet and creates PSpice simulation models of the magnetic part.
tools.usage: Start from the PSpice Accessories menu (Windows Start > Cadence > PSpice Accessories > Magnetic Parts Editor)
tools.example: New flyback transformer design > enter Vin range, output, frequency > pick core and wire > export the PSpice model and add the generated library to the profile.
tools.notes: Generated models use the CORE/K-coupled inductor constructs, so core-loss and saturation behaviour follow the PSpice magnetic models.

tools.name: DMI Template Code Generator (Device Model Interface)
tools.description: Generates C/C++ (and SystemC or Verilog-A) template code for a PSpice Device Model Interface model: part name and type, clocked or combinatorial interface, ports (typed in or read from a CSV), global and device parameters, and output DLL/log/directory. It writes a Visual Studio project (code folder) and a PSpice .lib model that already references the DLL to be built.
tools.usage: Model Editor (PSpice Accessories) > Model > DMI Template Code Generator

parameters.name: Part Details / Ports / Parameters / Output
parameters.description: The four sections of the generator form.

parameters.name: SYSTEMC environment variable
parameters.description: Needed for SystemC models; points to <CDSROOT>\tools\pspice\tclscripts\pspModelCreate\SystemC.

tools.example: Generate PWMControl, open code\PWMControl.vcxproj, build Release x64, implement pspPWMControl::evaluate in PWMControl_user.cpp, then add lib\PWMControl.lib to the profile.
tools.notes: Available since 17.2; model development needs PSpice Designer (or higher) and simulation of DMI models needs PSpice Designer Plus or Allegro PSpice Simulator. Reference docs: pspDMIRef.

tools.name: PSpice > Advanced Analysis > Sensitivity
tools.description: Advanced Analysis tool that ranks toleranced component parameters by their influence on measurements imported from PSpice. It reports absolute sensitivity (measurement change per one-unit parameter change) or relative sensitivity (percent change per one percent parameter change) with bar graphs, and can send the most sensitive parameters to the Optimizer.
tools.usage: Capture: PSpice > Advanced Analysis > Sensitivity; Specifications window: 'Click here to import a measurement created within PSpice'; Display > Absolute / Relative Sensitivity

parameters.name: Parameters window
parameters.description: Only parameters with tolerances (POSTOL/NEGTOL or model DEV/LOT) appear.

parameters.name: Send to Optimizer
parameters.description: Right-click selected parameters.

tools.example: Import Cutoff_Lowpass_3dB(V(out)), run, switch to Relative Sensitivity and send the top three resistors to the Optimizer.
tools.notes: Works on transient, DC sweep and AC sweep/noise profiles. Exclude parts with TOL_ON_OFF=OFF.

tools.name: PSpice > Advanced Analysis > Monte Carlo (yield analysis)
tools.description: Statistical analysis in Advanced Analysis that randomly varies toleranced parameters, evaluates imported measurements for every run and reports statistics, yield against specification limits, and PDF/CDF graphs. It is independent of the PSpice .MC settings.
tools.usage: PSpice > Advanced Analysis > Monte Carlo; Edit > Profile Settings > Monte Carlo tab

parameters.name: Number of Runs
parameters.description: 1 to 5000; run 1 uses nominal values.

parameters.name: Starting Run Number
parameters.description: Reproduce part of a previous run sequence with the same seed.

parameters.name: Random Seed Value
parameters.description: Same seed and properties give the same random sequence.

parameters.name: Number of Bins
parameters.description: Histogram divisions, 1 to 2000 (about runs/10).

tools.example: Import Max(V(out)) and Overshoot(V(out)), set min/max specs, 500 runs, seed 17, then read yield and the CDF graph.
tools.notes: Multi-run PSpice setups (parametric or temperature sweeps) are reduced to one run; for temperature lists the first value is used. Set Simulation data to Save None for thousands of runs to save disk space.

tools.name: Optimizer engines (Modified LSQ, Random, Discrete)
tools.description: Engines selectable in the Advanced Analysis Optimizer toolbar, normally used in the order Random, then Modified LSQ (MLSQ), then Discrete. Random picks values across the parameter range to find a starting point that avoids local minima and shows misfit and parameter history; Modified LSQ uses constrained and unconstrained minimisation to converge rapidly, treating specifications as goals or nonlinear constraints; Discrete rounds the optimised values to commercially available values from discrete tables and re-simulates.
tools.usage: PSpice > Advanced Analysis > Optimizer; engine drop-down on the toolbar; Discrete Table column per parameter

parameters.name: Specifications
parameters.description: Measurement specs (goal/constraint, min/max, weight) or curve-fit specs against reference waveforms.

parameters.name: Discrete Table
parameters.description: Built-in resistor/capacitor/inductor tolerance series or a user .table file.

tools.example: Modified LSQ to hit 10 kHz cutoff and 1 dB peaking, then switch to Discrete with a 1 % resistor table: 2.18113k becomes 2.21k.
tools.notes: Parameters come from PSpice > Advanced Analysis > Export Parameters to Optimizer, from the Parameters table ('Click here to import'), or from Sensitivity (Send to Optimizer). Analysis > Optimizer > Troubleshoot in PSpice compares a failed run with the nominal run. Earlier releases also offered a plain LSQ engine; check the engine drop-down of your release.

tools.name: PSpice > Advanced Analysis > Parametric Plot (Parametric Plotter)
tools.description: Sweeps any number of design and model parameters in any combination (nested), evaluates measurements for each combination and shows results in a spreadsheet and as plots in Probe. Sweep types are Discrete, Linear, LogarithmicDec and LogarithmicOct.
tools.usage: PSpice > Advanced Analysis > Parametric Plot (or open the .aap in Advanced Analysis and choose Parametric Plotter); Sweep Parameters: 'Click here to import a parameter from the design property map'

parameters.name: Discrete
parameters.description: Explicit value list, used in order.

parameters.name: Linear
parameters.description: Start, End, Step.

parameters.name: LogarithmicDec / LogarithmicOct
parameters.description: Start, End and points per decade/octave; factor = exp(ln(10)/N) or exp(ln(2)/N).

tools.example: Sweep R1 Linear 1k..10k step 1k and C1 Discrete 1n,2.2n,4.7n; measurement Bandwidth_Bandpass_3dB(V(out)); view the Results tab and Plot Information tab.
tools.notes: Requires a PSpice Advanced Analysis license. Only parameters defined on the schematic appear in the Parameter Selection dialog.

tools.name: PSpice > Advanced Analysis > Assign Tolerance
tools.description: Capture window for assigning positive/negative tolerances and FLAT or GAUSS distributions to standard parts (R, L, C, V, I, IGBT, JFET, BJT, MOSFET, K, D, S, GaAsFET), to model parameters and subcircuit model parameters (through Edit PSpice Model), and to global .PARAM parameters, so ordinary designs become Advanced Analysis-ready.
tools.usage: Capture: PSpice > Advanced Analysis > Assign Tolerance; Instance View tab (Global List / Instance List) and Model View tab; Apply

parameters.name: PosTol / NegTol
parameters.description: Percent tolerances.

parameters.name: Distribution
parameters.description: FLAT (default) or GAUSS.

parameters.name: Edit PSpice Model
parameters.description: Opens Model Editor to append DEV/<dist> tolerances to model parameters, e.g. Is=69.28E-18 DEV/UNIFORM 10%/1%.

tools.example: Global List > R: PosTol 1 %, NegTol 1 %, GAUSS > Apply; Instance List > C2: 5 %/5 % to override the global value.
tools.notes: Global tolerances are written to the [PSPICE_ADVANCED_ANALYSIS] section of PSpice.ini and apply to future designs too. Designs using this feature are not compatible with releases before SPB 17.20.011.

tools.name: VARIABLES part (Advanced Analysis design variables table)
tools.description: Part from the pspice_elem library that places a table of global Advanced Analysis variables on the schematic, such as RTOL for resistor tolerance, and smoke limits like RMAX and RTMAX. Editing a value in the table applies it to every applicable parameterised component unless an instance sets its own value.
tools.usage: Place > Part > add library pspice_elem > VARIABLES; double-click a value in the table > Display Properties > Value

parameters.name: RTOL
parameters.description: Positive and negative tolerance applied to all resistors.

parameters.name: RMAX / RTMAX
parameters.description: Resistor power and temperature smoke limits.

tools.example: Set RTOL to 5 in the table so every Advanced Analysis resistor gets a 5 % tolerance for Sensitivity and Monte Carlo.
tools.notes: Instance-level parameter values override the table.

tools.name: TOL_ON_OFF (property)
tools.description: Instance or hierarchical-block property that includes (ON, the default when absent) or excludes (OFF) a component's tolerances from Sensitivity and Monte Carlo in Advanced Analysis. On a hierarchical block it overrides the setting of every component inside.
tools.usage: Property Editor: TOL_ON_OFF = ON | OFF
tools.example: Set TOL_ON_OFF=OFF on the reference-voltage hierarchical block to study only the amplifier tolerances.

tools.name: Smoke derating (No Derating, Standard Derating, Custom Derating Files)
tools.description: Derating options of the Advanced Analysis Smoke stress test. Smoke compares average, RMS and peak stresses with each part's maximum operating conditions multiplied by a derating factor; the default No Derating uses 100 %, Standard Derating applies Cadence's standard factors, and custom .drt files supply your own. Results show % Max for every parameter.
tools.usage: Advanced Analysis Smoke: right-click > Derating > No Derating | Standard Derating | Custom Derating Files (browse to .drt)

parameters.name: MOC
parameters.description: Maximum operating condition from the part's smoke parameters (e.g. POWER=RMAX).

parameters.name: % Derating
parameters.description: Safe operating limit = MOC x % derating.

tools.example: Run Smoke on the transient profile, right-click > Derating > Standard Derating, then sort by % Max to find overstressed capacitors.
tools.notes: Only parts with smoke parameters are checked; average and peak values are the meaningful ones for most parameters.

tools.name: .aap / .drt / .table / .prp (Advanced Analysis files)
tools.description: Files used by PSpice Advanced Analysis: the .aap Advanced Analysis profile stores tool setups and results (together with the PSpice .sim profiles it references); .drt files hold custom Smoke derating factors; .table files hold discrete value tables for the Optimizer's Discrete engine; .prp device property files describe model parameters, tolerances and smoke data for parameterised parts.
tools.usage: File > Save in Advanced Analysis writes <design>.aap; .drt via Smoke > Custom Derating Files; .table via the Optimizer Discrete Table column; .prp in the library folders
tools.example: Commit amp.aap, company_derate.drt and e96.table with the project so colleagues get identical Advanced Analysis setups.
tools.notes: Distribution files for Monte Carlo live in <install>\tools\pspice\library\distribution unless DISTRIBUTION_DIRNAME is set in the PSPICE_ADVANCED ANALYSIS section of pspice.ini (relative to LIBPATH).
